newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Meridor says no choice but to cut budget.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Meridor says no choice but to cut budget.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor has dismissed threats by coalition legislators to allow the government to fall rather than approve the Treasury's 1997 budget proposal.
"I don't understand how bringing down the government will help. If there's a new government, it will also need to cut spending," Meridor said in an interview with Israel Radio.

Meridor was responding to threats by Maxim Levy, a member of parliament in the Likud's Gesher faction, who said on Wednesday that the party was letting down its voters with the proposed budget and should not continue governing.
Levy and other legislators say the the Treasury's proposed budget cuts, which are expected to amount to around seven billion shekels, will fall disproportionately on lower-income groups.
Meridor denied the budget would hurt the disadvantaged and reiterated earlier warnings that without cuts the ensuing economic crisis would hit them hardest.
"Taking care of the weaker classes requires first of all preventing an (economic) crisis," he said.

The government says the spending reductions are needed to keep the budget deficit to a targeted 2.8 percent of gross domestic product next year. Widening deficits in the last two years have fuelled a growing current account deficit.

Meridor denied that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was not fully backing him on the controversial cuts. He dismissed speculation that he would resign if parliament does not approve the budget by the December 31 deadline.
Asked if he would still be finance minister on January 1 if the Knesset rejected the budget, he responded: "I suggest we meet after the budget has passed and ask me that question again."
